title: Scaling Laws & Capabilities
scopeHtml: Scaling-law intuitions, compute-optimal vs overtrained models, emergence, benchmarks and contamination, training-cost intuition, the data wall, and inference-time scaling.

questions.promptHtml: What is a neural scaling law, and how did the Chinchilla result differ from the earlier Kaplan result?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know why "bigger model" stopped being the only lever, and whether you can state the finding precisely instead of "more data is better".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A scaling law says pretraining loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters N, training tokens D and compute C. Kaplan et al. (2020) concluded that for a fixed compute budget you should mostly grow the model and train it on relatively modest data, stopping before convergence. Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) redid the fits with proper learning-rate schedules per run and found N and D should scale roughly in equal proportion, about 20 tokens per parameter. Their 70B model trained on about 4x more data than the 280B Gopher, at the same compute, beat it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A power law means L(N) ≈ (Nc/N)^alpha: a straight line on log-log axes. Kaplan reported this across more than seven orders of magnitude of compute, and that architecture details (depth vs width) mattered little compared with scale.

The disagreement is about the allocation question: given compute C, split it between N and D.

C ≈ 6 * N * D          (training FLOPs: ~2ND forward + ~4ND backward)

Kaplan  : N_opt grows fast with C, D grows slowly   -> big model, little data
Chinchilla: N_opt ∝ C^0.5, D_opt ∝ C^0.5            -> double N => double D

A commonly cited cause of the gap (verify against the Chinchilla paper's appendix): Kaplan used a fixed LR schedule length for all runs, which penalised the longer runs and made extra data look less useful. Chinchilla matched the cosine schedule to each run's length.

Consequence: GPT-3 (175B, about 300B tokens, a commonly cited figure, verify) was far from compute-optimal; the same compute buys a smaller model trained longer with a lower loss.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import math
def chinchilla_opt(C, tokens_per_param=20):
    # C = 6*N*D and D = k*N  =>  C = 6*k*N^2
    N = math.sqrt(C / (6 * tokens_per_param))
    return N, tokens_per_param * N

N, D = chinchilla_opt(5.88e23)   # ~Chinchilla's budget
print(f"{N:.2e} params, {D:.2e} tokens")  # ~7.0e10 params, ~1.4e12 tokens

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Chinchilla proved small models are better". It says nothing about inference cost; it optimises training loss per training FLOP.
  • Quoting "20 tokens per parameter" as a law of nature. It is a fit that depends on data quality and the fitting method.
  • Forgetting that loss is not downstream task quality.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does 6ND come from? → about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token forward, about 4 backward.
  2. Does the law predict benchmark scores? → Loss yes (smooth); downstream tasks only indirectly (see Q115, Q123).
  3. Why did the two papers disagree? → Different experimental protocol, mainly LR schedule and the range of model sizes fitted.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Chinchilla says train on more data." Senior: states the C=6ND allocation problem, the 20:1 heuristic, why Kaplan got it wrong, and that it optimises training compute, not lifetime cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams budgeting a from-scratch or continued-pretraining run use these fits to pick model size for a fixed GPU budget before committing millions.

questions.subtopic: Reading loss curves and power laws
questions.promptHtml: If a scaling-law plot shows loss falling as a straight line on log-log axes, what can and can't you conclude from it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests basic quantitative literacy about the field's central chart.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A straight line on log-log means a power law: each constant multiplicative increase in compute gives a constant multiplicative drop in the reducible loss. It means returns diminish in absolute terms but are predictable, and that you can extrapolate small runs. It does not tell me the loss floor is zero, that downstream skills improve smoothly, or that the trend holds outside the fitted range.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fitted form (Chinchilla-style): L(N,D) = E + A/N^a + B/D^b. E is the irreducible loss (entropy of the text); the other two are the reducible parts from finite model and finite data.

Worked example: suppose reducible loss = 10 * C^-0.05. 10x compute multiplies it by 10^-0.05 = 0.891, an 11% cut. 100x gives 0.794, a 21% cut. Each decade of compute costs 10x more money for the same proportional gain. That is the "diminishing returns but predictable" shape.

Where to be careful: (1) plots often show reducible loss or loss minus a fitted floor; raw loss will curve; (2) loss is nats/bits per token averaged over a particular data mix, so it is not comparable across tokenizers; (3) extrapolating two orders of magnitude beyond the fit is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
C = np.array([1e18, 1e19, 1e20, 1e21])
L = np.array([3.4, 3.05, 2.75, 2.5])           # example numbers
E = 1.7                                         # assumed floor; fit it in practice
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log(C), np.log(L - E), 1)
print(slope)                                    # the exponent, negative
pred = np.exp(intercept) * (1e23) ** slope + E  # extrapolation: treat as a guess

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fitting a line to raw loss without subtracting the floor, which biases the exponent.
  • Comparing losses across different tokenizers or data mixes.
  • Treating extrapolation as a guarantee.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is loss per token not comparable across tokenizers? → Different tokens carry different amounts of text; use bits-per-byte.
  2. What does the irreducible term E represent? → Entropy of natural text, which no model can beat.
  3. Can a power law hold forever? → No; data limits, noise floor and optimiser effects bend it (see Q118).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "loss goes down with scale." Senior: computes the proportional gain per decade, names the floor, units and extrapolation risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Small-scale ablation runs (10-100x cheaper) are used to pick data mixes; teams that skip the floor term misjudge which mix wins at full scale.

questions.promptHtml: Given a budget of 1e24 training FLOPs, how would you estimate the compute-optimal model size and token count, and how many GPU-hours is that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Back-of-envelope fluency is a core senior skill; it shows you can sanity-check a vendor's or colleague's plan.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use C ≈ 6ND with D ≈ 20N. So C = 120 N², N = sqrt(1e24/120) ≈ 91B parameters and D ≈ 1.8T tokens. For GPU time, divide by realistic sustained FLOPs: H100 peak dense BF16 is on the order of 1e15 FLOP/s (verify spec), and large runs often reach roughly 30-45% utilisation, so about 4e14 effective. That is 2.5e9 GPU-seconds, about 700k GPU-hours.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
C = 6 N D,  D = 20 N  ->  N = sqrt(C/120)
N = sqrt(1e24/120) = sqrt(8.33e21) = 9.1e10
D = 20 * 9.1e10    = 1.83e12
GPU-sec = 1e24 / (4e14) = 2.5e9  -> /3600 = 6.9e5 GPU-hours
At $2/GPU-hr (verify market rate): ~$1.4M; at $4: ~$2.8M

The 6ND rule ignores attention FLOPs (matters at long context), embedding parameters and activation recomputation (gradient checkpointing adds roughly another forward pass, about +33% compute). MFU (model FLOPs utilisation) is the main uncertainty: interconnect, pipeline bubbles, data loading and failures all reduce it. Hardware cost is also only part: failed-run restarts, ablations and data work often multiply the headline number several times.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def plan(C, mfu=0.4, peak=1e15, usd_hr=2.0, k=20):
    N = (C / (6*k)) ** 0.5
    D = k * N
    gpu_hours = C / (peak * mfu) / 3600
    return N, D, gpu_hours, gpu_hours * usd_hr
print(plan(1e24))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using peak FLOPs as achieved FLOPs.
  • Counting only the final run, not ablations and restarts.
  • Forgetting MoE: use active parameters in 6ND (see C1 T2 chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would 8-bit/FP8 training change it? → Higher peak throughput, but check the quality and stability trade-offs.
  2. What if you must serve to many users? → Compute-optimal is wrong target; see Q114.
  3. How would you validate the 20:1 for your data? → Run IsoFLOP sweeps at small scale and fit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names the formula. Senior: does the arithmetic live, includes MFU and hidden costs, flags assumptions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sized a continued-pretraining job from peak FLOPs and was 2.5x over on cluster time because MFU was 16% due to slow data loading.

questions.promptHtml: Why do modern open models like Llama 3 8B train far past the Chinchilla-optimal token count?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates "training-optimal" from "lifetime-cost-optimal" thinking, which drives every model-choice decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Chinchilla minimises loss for a given training budget. But a model is trained once and served billions of times, and inference cost scales with parameters. So it pays to spend extra training compute on a smaller model to reach the quality of a larger one. Meta reported training Llama 3 8B on about 15T tokens, roughly 1,900 tokens per parameter versus the 20 heuristic, with loss still improving log-linearly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lifetime cost = training + inference. Training is about 6ND FLOPs; inference is about 2N FLOPs per generated or processed token. If a model serves T tokens over its life:

total = 6*N*D + 2*N*T

For N=8B, D=15T: training = 68e915e12 = 7.2e23 FLOPs. If it serves T=1e15 tokens (a busy product, illustrative), inference = 28e91e15 = 1.6e25, over 20x the training. Making N smaller by 2x saves far more at serving than the extra training tokens cost. This is why optimising for N*(D+T/3) rather than D alone moves the optimum toward small N, large D.

Limits: returns per extra token keep diminishing, data quality and the data wall (Q118) cap it, and a small model has lower ceilings on hard reasoning tasks no matter how long it trains.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def lifetime_flops(N, D, T): return 6*N*D + 2*N*T
big   = lifetime_flops(70e9, 1.4e12, 1e15)
small = lifetime_flops(8e9, 15e12, 1e15)
print(big/small)   # ~ 7x more lifetime compute for 70B vs 8B at this demand; quality differs

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling it "ignoring Chinchilla"; it is optimising a different objective.
  • Assuming the small model matches the big one on everything.
  • Ignoring that inference is memory-bandwidth bound, so FLOP counts understate the advantage of small models (see C2).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. At what traffic does overtraining stop paying? → When T is small relative to D, e.g. a rarely used internal model; then Chinchilla-optimal wins.
  2. How does this affect fine-tuning choice? → Small overtrained base models are strong starting points for narrow tasks.
  3. Does distillation change the picture? → Yes: a big teacher can supply better tokens than raw web data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "more data is better." Senior: writes the lifetime-cost equation and says when it flips.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Picking an 8B-class model over a 70B-class one for 80% of traffic is this argument expressed as a routing rule.

questions.promptHtml: What are "emergent abilities", and why do some researchers say they are a mirage?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you reason about metrics and measurement rather than repeating hype, and whether you can plan around unpredictable capability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Emergent abilities are skills that appear absent in small models and then jump sharply at some scale. Schaeffer et al. argue many of those jumps come from the metric: exact-match or all-or-nothing scores are nonlinear in per-token accuracy, so smooth underlying improvement looks like a sudden leap. With continuous metrics like token-level log-likelihood the curves are smooth. The honest position: some of it is metric artefact, but for practical purposes capability on a specific task can still be hard to predict in advance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Toy math: a task needs a 10-token exact answer. If per-token accuracy p rises smoothly from 0.5 to 0.95, exact match is p^10: 0.001 to 0.60. The curve looks flat at 0 and then shoots up, while p changed gradually. Use partial credit or per-token likelihood and the jump disappears.

What the critique does not settle: (1) the question is still whether a given task becomes usable at the scale you can afford; (2) multi-step reasoning and tool use may genuinely depend on compounding reliability; (3) few-shot and chain-of-thought effects depend on training recipe, not scale alone. The debate also affects safety forecasting: if capability isn't predictable, small-scale evals may miss risks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
p = np.linspace(0.5, 0.95, 10)
print(np.round(p**10, 3))   # exact-match over 10 tokens: looks like a sudden jump
print(np.round(p, 3))       # per-token accuracy: smooth

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "emergence is fake". The paper argues many reported cases are metric-driven, not all.
  • Citing emergence to justify "just wait for a bigger model" without testing.
  • Ignoring that your own product metric may be an all-or-nothing one.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test for emergence in your task? → Evaluate with continuous and partial-credit metrics across model sizes.
  2. Why does it matter for product planning? → A pass-rate metric can hide steady progress, or hide a cliff; track both.
  3. How does it relate to chain-of-thought? → CoT gains tend to appear at larger scales, so check each size with your prompt.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: repeats either side. Senior: shows the p^k arithmetic and links it to how they design eval metrics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent pipeline whose end-to-end success looked flat across model sizes was actually improving per-step; success is a product of steps.

questions.promptHtml: What are benchmark contamination and saturation, and how do they make leaderboard numbers unreliable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Model selection and vendor claims rest on benchmarks; seniors must know how they fail.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Contamination means test items, or near-copies, leaked into training data, so the score measures memorisation. Saturation means top models cluster near the ceiling, so the benchmark can't tell them apart and label errors dominate the remaining gap. Both inflate or flatten the signal, so I treat public benchmarks as a coarse filter and decide with my own held-out task evals.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Contamination routes: the benchmark itself is on the web (GitHub, forums, papers); paraphrased or translated copies; training on synthetic data derived from benchmark-like items; deliberate or accidental tuning on the test set. Detection: n-gram overlap (e.g. 13-gram) between training and test (needs the training data, which closed vendors don't share), perplexity or completion-order tests (a model that reproduces items verbatim or prefers the canonical order has probably seen them), comparing performance on original vs rewritten items, and dynamic benchmarks refreshed after the model's cutoff.

Saturation: when top scores are around 90%+, a 1-point gap is within noise and mislabeled items; that is a few hundred questions. Check confidence intervals: with n=1,000 and p=0.9, the standard error is sqrt(0.9*0.1/1000)=0.95 points, so a 95% interval is about ±1.9.

Other issues: prompt format, few-shot count, and answer-extraction differences change scores by several points, so numbers from different reports are not comparable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def ngram_overlap(test_text, train_ngrams, n=13):
    toks = test_text.split()
    grams = {" ".join(toks[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(toks)-n+1)}
    return len(grams & train_ngrams) / max(len(grams), 1)
# flag items with overlap > 0 for manual review

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trusting a vendor-reported number with no stated prompt, shots and decoding settings.
  • Treating small deltas as real without confidence intervals.
  • Assuming "no overlap found" proves cleanliness; paraphrases evade n-grams.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect it without the training set? → Rewrite items and compare, check memorised completions, use post-cutoff tasks.
  2. What replaces a saturated benchmark? → Harder or newer sets, private held-out evals, human-preference or task-specific evals (see the evals track).
  3. Why can a private eval go stale too? → Once reused many times for selection, you overfit to it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "benchmarks can be gamed." Senior: gives detection methods, the CI arithmetic, and a policy of using a private eval for decisions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A model that topped a public coding benchmark scored 15 points lower on a team's internal repo tasks.

questions.contextHtml: A vendor's launch post says their new model "beats GPT-class models on MMLU, HumanEval and GSM8K" and shows a bar chart: new model 88.5, competitor 87.0 on MMLU. Footnotes: new model "5-shot, best of 3 runs"; competitor number "from the competitor's technical report". Your VP wants to switch a support-classification workload (2M requests/day, mean 900 input tokens) to it because it is also "30% cheaper per token". MMLU has about 14k questions. You have 400 labelled tickets from production.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do before agreeing to switch?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "88.5 beats 87.0, and it is cheaper, so switch." It ignores protocol mismatch, noise, relevance and total cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the task really need (classification, extraction)? What is the cost of a wrong label? Is "30% cheaper" input, output, or both, and is it per token of the same tokenizer? What latency and data-handling terms apply?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No production change. I'd run a shadow evaluation on the 400 tickets, which costs almost nothing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the 1.5-point gap is within noise or protocol difference (best-of-3 vs reported single run); (b) MMLU is saturated and unrelated to ticket classification; (c) possible contamination; (d) per-token price not comparable because of tokenizer differences.
  4. How I'd verify each: Gap noise: n=14k gives SE about sqrt(0.88*0.12/14000)=0.27 points, so 1.5 is not pure sampling noise, but the best-of-3 vs single-run mismatch can easily exceed that. Run both models on the 400 tickets with the same prompt, report accuracy with a bootstrap CI (n=400 gives about ±3 points at 90%, so I'd expand the set to 1,000+ if the models are close). Count tokens of the same 900-token prompt with each model's tokenizer to compare real cost per request.
  5. Root cause: The chart compares non-equivalent protocols, and the metric isn't the task.
  6. Fix: Decide on the private eval plus cost per correct label. Example: if the new model costs 30% less per token but its tokenizer yields 15% more tokens, the real saving is about 0.7*1.15=0.805, so 19.5%.
  7. Prevention: Keep a versioned private eval set and a standard harness so every candidate is compared under one prompt.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't run a big migration on public numbers; I also wouldn't ignore the vendor, since a pilot costs little.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The 400-ticket accuracies are 91.0% vs 90.5%. → Within noise; decide on cost, latency and robustness, or gather more data.
  • The vendor won't disclose training data. → Treat contamination as unknown; rely on post-cutoff tickets.
  • Latency is 2x higher. → Quantify against the SLA; the saving may not be worth it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team switched models on the strength of a chart and found support-category accuracy dropped four points on rare classes the benchmark never covered; the rollback cost two weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the chart at face value.
  • Hire: asks for a private eval and notes protocol mismatch.
  • Strong hire: quantifies noise and CI, tokenizer-adjusted cost, and defines a decision rule.

questions.promptHtml: What is the "data wall", and what are the realistic ways labs respond to it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about the constraint that limits pretraining scaling, beyond hype.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compute-optimal training wants tokens to grow in step with model size, but the stock of high-quality public human text is finite. Epoch AI's 2022 estimate was that training sets could reach the size of the available public human text between 2026 and 2032, sooner if models are overtrained. Responses: multiple epochs on the same data, better filtering and quality weighting, synthetic data, multimodal and code data, private or licensed data, and shifting compute to post-training and inference time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why it bites: D=20N means a 1T-parameter compute-optimal model wants 20T tokens, and overtrained models want far more. Web crawls hold lots of text, but after dedup, quality filtering and licensing the usable pool is much smaller.

Levers and their limits:

  • Repeated epochs: research on data-constrained scaling suggests a few epochs (roughly up to 4, verify) behave almost like fresh data, with returns decaying after.
  • Synthetic data: helps for code, math and verifiable domains; risks model collapse and narrow distributions if unfiltered (covered in the training-stages chunk).
  • Quality over quantity: aggressive filtering often beats raw size at fixed compute.
  • Verifiable-reward RL and test-time compute: scale with compute, not human text.

Caveat: forecasts depend on assumptions (what counts as usable, growth in overtraining) and have wide ranges; I'd quote the range, not a date.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# toy: how many tokens does a compute-optimal run need?
for N in (7e9, 70e9, 400e9, 1e12):
    print(f"{N:.0e} params -> {20*N:.1e} tokens at 20:1; {200*N:.1e} at 200:1 (overtrained)")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Stating a single year as fact.
  • Treating the wall as hard; it moves with data quality and new sources.
  • Assuming synthetic data is free of failure modes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does overtraining hasten the wall? → It consumes tokens faster than the compute-optimal rule.
  2. Are repeated epochs safe for LLMs? → A few are close to fresh data; many risk memorisation.
  3. How does it shape product strategy? → Capability gains shift toward post-training, tools and inference-time compute.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "we'll run out of internet." Senior: ties D=20N arithmetic to the pool, lists levers with their limits, and quotes forecast ranges.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: For teams, it shows up as domain data being the scarce asset: your proprietary corpus matters more than model size for fine-tuning.

questions.promptHtml: What is inference-time (test-time) scaling, and when is it better than using a bigger model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reasoning models change cost/latency design; seniors must reason about when extra thinking pays.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Instead of making the model bigger, you spend more compute per query: sample many answers and pick one (best-of-N, majority vote), use a verifier or reward model to search, or let the model generate a long chain of thought. Snell et al. (2024) found that allocating test-time compute adaptively per prompt can beat best-of-N by over 4x efficiency, and that on problems where a small model has non-trivial success, extra test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched comparison. It helps on checkable, multi-step tasks and doesn't fix missing knowledge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanics: (1) parallel: N samples plus a selector; (2) sequential: longer reasoning, self-revision; (3) search: tree or beam over steps scored by a process verifier. Reasoning models are trained (RL with verifiable rewards, verify current recipes) to use long chains productively.

Cost: a 5,000-token reasoning trace at 80 tokens/s is about 62 s of decode; tokens are billed as output tokens even when hidden. Compare per-query cost: 8B model with best-of-8 = 8 * 8B decode vs one 70B decode: similar FLOPs, but parallel samples batch well while a bigger model's quality ceiling differs.

When it fails: knowledge gaps (model doesn't know the fact), tasks with no reliable verifier (majority vote of wrong answers amplifies the error), easy tasks (wasted cost), and strict latency budgets.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from collections import Counter
def majority_vote(sample_fn, prompt, n=8):
    answers = [sample_fn(prompt, temperature=0.8) for _ in range(n)]
    return Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0][0]
# works for tasks with short canonical answers; needs temperature>0 for diversity

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it on tasks without a verifier or a canonical answer format.
  • Forgetting hidden reasoning tokens in the cost estimate.
  • Setting temperature 0 with best-of-N (identical samples).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can small model + search beat a large model? → Verification is easier than generation, and compute is spent where the question is hard.
  2. How do you set the budget per query? → Route by difficulty estimate; cap reasoning tokens.
  3. How does this affect serving? → Longer decodes raise KV-cache and latency pressure (see the inference track).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "reasoning models think longer." Senior: separates parallel/sequential/search, bases on verifier availability, and prices it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team routing only hard tickets to a reasoning model cut spend versus sending all traffic there while keeping quality.

questions.contextHtml: A startup CEO asks whether you should "train our own 70B model from scratch" because API spend is $180k/month on a document-extraction product (about 3B tokens/day total). You have 128 H100s on offer at $2.5/GPU-hour (verify), a 1.5T-token licensed/proprietary corpus of mixed quality, and no prior pretraining experience. An open 70B model scores 94% on your internal extraction eval; the API model scores 96%.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate the cost and give a recommendation.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Training is expensive, just use the API," with no numbers, or "70B x 1.4T tokens, easy."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 2-point gap business-relevant? What are latency and data-residency constraints? What is the growth in volume? Is the corpus in-domain for extraction?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing is on fire; first quote the cheaper options: caching, batching, a smaller model for easy documents, prompt trimming.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fine-tuning an open model closes the 2-point gap at 1% of the cost; (b) routing cuts API spend 40-60%; (c) from-scratch pretraining is not justified.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute: C = 670e91.4e12 = 5.9e23 FLOPs. At 40% MFU on ~1e15 peak (assumed) = 4e14 FLOP/s per GPU; 128 GPUs = 5.1e16 FLOP/s. Time = 5.9e23/5.1e16 = 1.15e7 s, about 133 days. GPU-hours = 12824133 = about 408k; at $2.5 = about $1.0M for one clean run. Realistically 2-4x for restarts, ablations, data work, and 2-3 engineers for months. Break-even against $180k/month: over $2M / $180k = 11+ months, before serving costs of 70B (about 4 H100s per replica).
  5. Root cause: The real problem is a 2-point quality gap and API spend, not lack of a base model.
  6. Fix: Short term: fine-tune the open 70B (or a smaller one) with LoRA on labelled extractions, evaluate on the internal set; route easy docs to a small model. Long term: revisit pretraining only for a defensible data advantage.
  7. Prevention: Track cost per successfully extracted document; re-run the build-vs-buy sheet quarterly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't pretrain from scratch with a team that has never done it: MFU of 16% instead of 40% would double the bill and a loss spike can burn a week.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Spend grows 10x. → Self-hosting a fine-tuned model becomes attractive; still no need to pretrain.
  • The corpus is exclusive and huge. → Consider continued pretraining of an open base on it, a fraction of the cost.
  • The CEO wants a "defensible moat". → Moat is data and evals, not weights.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team budgeted a run from peak FLOPs and discovered mid-run that cluster interconnect gave 18% MFU; the project was cancelled after burning most of the quarter's compute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers or a wildly wrong estimate.
  • Hire: correct 6ND estimate with GPU-hours and cost, and recommends fine-tuning.
  • Strong hire: includes MFU/restart/staff multipliers, break-even, serving cost, and cheaper alternatives.

questions.contextHtml: Your team fine-tuned a 7B model on 200k synthetic coding tasks generated by a larger model. Internal benchmark: 71% pass@1 on a public 500-problem coding set, up from 52% for the base. In a pilot with real customer repos, pass rate on 300 tasks is 49%. Marketing already published "71%". A teammate notes the generator model was prompted with "problems in the style of" the public set, and the training JSON has a field source_hint containing problem titles. Dedup was done by exact string match only.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened, how do you confirm, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Collect more data and retrain." It never questions the benchmark number.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which exact prompts went to the generator? Do any training items share titles, function signatures or tests with the 500? Were hyperparameters tuned against the benchmark? Was the pilot sample representative?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Retract or caveat the 71% publicly; freeze reporting of that number.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) near-duplicate leakage via generator style prompting; (b) benchmark overfit through repeated checkpoint selection; (c) distribution shift between clean benchmark problems and messy repos; (d) pilot harness differences (red herring candidate: prompt template differences).
  4. How I'd verify each: Fuzzy dedup: MinHash/embedding similarity of every training item against the 500 test problems, plus 13-gram overlap; manually inspect top matches. Evaluate base and tuned model on a fresh set of problems written after generation. Compare per-item performance on high-overlap vs low-overlap test items. Run the pilot tasks through the benchmark harness format to exclude format differences.
  5. Root cause: Synthetic generation conditioned on the test set leaked paraphrases; exact-match dedup missed them; the benchmark was also used for checkpoint selection.
  6. Fix: Remove matches above a similarity threshold, retrain, report on a held-out never-seen set plus the customer-repo set; show the number with a confidence interval (n=300 at 49%: SE about 2.9 points).
  7. Prevention: Never put test content or titles in generator prompts; fuzzy decontamination in the data pipeline; hold-out sets stored separately and touched once; report-level checklist.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't just drop the benchmark: keep it as a regression check but not as the headline.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• After decontamination the score is 58%. → Report 58%; the 13-point gap was leakage.
  • Overlap is low but the gap persists. → Distribution shift; invest in repo-style training data.
  • Legal asks whether you can still claim the base's improvement. → Only with the clean eval.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A synthetic-data pipeline reused a seed list that included benchmark titles; the leak was found only because per-item results showed suspiciously perfect scores on a cluster of problems.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retrains without checking leakage.
  • Hire: identifies contamination and does overlap analysis.
  • Strong hire: fuzzy dedup, fresh eval, CI, communication correction, and process changes.

questions.contextHtml: A chat product serves 40M requests/day, average 1,200 input and 300 output tokens. Option A: hosted 70B-class open model on H100s. Option B: an 8B-class overtrained model, fine-tuned on your domain. Offline eval on 1,000 held-out conversations (judge-scored 1-5): A 4.35, B 4.12, with per-category gaps largest on multi-step reasoning (A 4.1 vs B 3.4). Estimated serving cost: A $0.60 per 1M tokens, B $0.09 per 1M tokens (assumed, verify with your own benchmarks). Product team says users complain mostly about wrong answers on hard questions, which are 12% of traffic.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you pick, and how do you justify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bigger is better, take A", or "cheaper, take B", without computing or segmenting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How is "hard" defined and can it be detected? Latency targets? Is the judge calibrated against humans? What is the revenue impact of a bad answer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No incident; run a pilot with routing on 5% traffic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the 0.23 mean gap hides a concentrated deficit on hard queries; (b) a router can send the 12% to A; (c) B plus test-time compute could close part of the gap.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cost: tokens/day = 40M1,500 = 60B. A = 60,000 M tokens$0.60 = $36k/day (about $1.08M/month). B = $5.4k/day. Routing 12% to A, 88% to B: 0.1236k+0.885.4k = 4.32k+4.75k = $9.1k/day, about 75% cheaper than A-only. Quality: per-category evals, router accuracy on labelled hard cases (a misrouted hard query gets B's 3.4), pairwise human check of a sample.
  5. Root cause: Averages mask the heterogeneous difficulty; capability gaps appear on reasoning, as scaling intuitions predict.
  6. Fix: Cascade: B first, escalate to A on low confidence or detected reasoning intent; optionally best-of-N on B for borderline cases.
  7. Prevention: Per-segment dashboards, router drift monitoring, periodic re-eval when either model is updated.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't trust a single judge score, and I wouldn't pick based on the average.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Router accuracy is only 80%. → Quantify expected quality: 20% of hard queries get B quality; maybe widen escalation threshold.
  • Traffic grows 10x. → Absolute savings grow; serving A for the 12% still costs about $0.9M/month at that scale under these assumptions.
  • A is deprecated by the vendor. → Another reason for the abstraction layer and eval harness.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's average-score comparison favored the cheap model; after segmenting, all the regression sat in the 10% of queries that drove support escalations.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by average or by size alone.
  • Hire: computes costs and proposes routing.
  • Strong hire: segments, quantifies router error, includes monitoring and deprecation risk.

questions.promptHtml: Scaling laws predict loss well. Why can't you simply use them to predict what a model will be able to do, and where do they break?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes depth: knowing the gap between a smooth loss curve and product-relevant capability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Laws are fit to next-token loss on a specific data distribution. Task performance is a nonlinear, sometimes thresholded function of loss and depends on data mix, post-training and the metric. Extrapolating beyond the fitted range is also risky: data limits, optimiser instabilities, changing data quality and architecture changes shift the curve. So I use laws for planning compute and ranking small-scale ablations, and I validate capabilities directly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers of translation: compute -> loss (well-behaved power law) -> per-skill accuracy (a task-specific curve, often sigmoid-shaped in log-compute) -> product outcome (depends on prompts, tools, post-training).

Breakage points:

  • Distribution: the law holds for the training distribution; a model's loss on code can improve while on rare languages it doesn't.
  • Fit sensitivity: exponents depend on method; Kaplan vs Chinchilla differed materially on the allocation.
  • Regime change: repeated data, synthetic data and RL post-training have different scaling behaviour from web pretraining.
  • Inverse or non-monotonic scaling on some tasks was reported in the literature (verify specific cases such as the Inverse Scaling Prize).
  • Post-training can shift capability by more than a 2x increase in pretraining compute on some tasks.

Practical use: fit on runs at 1/100 to 1/1000 of target compute, extrapolate 1-2 orders of magnitude, hold a confidence band, and verify with one intermediate run.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# bootstrap the uncertainty on an extrapolated loss
import numpy as np
def extrapolate(C, L, target, E, n_boot=500):
    preds=[]
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        idx=np.random.choice(len(C), len(C))
        if len(set(idx))<3: continue
        s,i=np.polyfit(np.log(C[idx]), np.log(L[idx]-E), 1)
        preds.append(np.exp(i)*target**s+E)
    return np.percentile(preds,[5,50,95])

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating "lower loss" with "better on my task".
  • Extrapolating many orders of magnitude from three small points.
  • Ignoring post-training effects.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do labs predict capability before a big run? → Fit loss laws and, for some tasks, task-level predictions on small runs; accuracy is limited (verify published examples).
  2. Why are post-trained model comparisons different from base ones? → Instruction tuning and RL change behaviour not captured by pretrain loss.
  3. How do you rank data mixes cheaply? → Small proxy runs, with caution on rank flips at scale.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "laws predict performance." Senior: lays out the layers of translation and what to measure directly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that chose a base model purely by perplexity found it lagged on instruction-following tasks after tuning.

questions.contextHtml: You run a support assistant on a standard chat model: p50 latency 2.1 s, p95 4.5 s, cost $0.004 per request at 5M requests/day. You A/B test a reasoning model on 5% traffic: resolution accuracy rises from 78% to 86% on a 2,000-case eval, but p50 latency becomes 14 s, p95 41 s, and cost per request $0.031. Output tokens jumped from 350 to about 4,200 (including hidden reasoning). Timeouts at the gateway (30 s) hit 7% of reasoning requests. Product wants a 100% rollout next week.
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide and de-risk the rollout?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "8 points is huge, ship it" or "too slow, reject".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is a resolved ticket worth versus an escalated one? Which request types gain? Is the interface streaming? Can the reasoning budget be capped?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the A/B at 5% and raise gateway timeouts for that path only; fall back to the standard model on timeout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) gains concentrate in a minority of complex cases; (b) most traffic is simple and pays 8x for no gain; (c) timeouts bias the measured accuracy (red herring: eval set may skew hard).
  4. How I'd verify each: Cost at full rollout: 5M*$0.031 = $155k/day vs $20k/day now, +$135k/day. Gain: 8 points on 5M = 400k more resolutions/day; if each avoided escalation saves $0.60, that is $240k/day, so it can pay, but only if the effect holds on real mix. Bucket the eval by category and by baseline confidence; measure uplift per bucket; check the 7% timeouts' effect on accuracy.
  5. Root cause: Reasoning tokens (4,200 vs 350 output) drive both cost and latency roughly linearly in decode time.
  6. Fix: Route: easy intents to the standard model, hard or low-confidence cases to the reasoning model, with a reasoning-effort/token cap; stream a progress message; async path for slow cases.
  7. Prevention: Per-route cost/latency/quality dashboards, budget alarms, regression eval each model version.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't flip everything at 100%; I wouldn't hide the p95 behind the p50.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Routing the hardest 20% captures 70% of the gain. → Cost: 20% of $155k plus 80% of $20k = $47k/day, a good point.
  • Provider rate limits tokens/minute. → Reasoning traffic spikes tokens; request quota first.
  • Users abandon after 8 s. → Measure abandonment; consider asynchronous replies.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team enabled a reasoning model globally and the monthly bill grew 7x in a week; routing by intent recovered most of the gain at a fifth of the cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: decides on accuracy alone.
  • Hire: computes cost/latency and proposes routing.
  • Strong hire: values uplift in dollars, segments by bucket, handles timeouts, quotas and monitoring.
